levels.title: First Steps
levels.blurb: Meet TypeScript and add your very first type annotations to everyday JavaScript.

levels.title: Shaping Data
levels.blurb: Describe objects, arrays, and tuples with interfaces and type aliases.

levels.title: Unions & Narrowing
levels.blurb: Let a value be one of several types, then teach TypeScript which one it is.

levels.title: Functions & Generics
levels.blurb: Type your functions, tame `any` with `unknown`, and write reusable generic code.

levels.title: Pro Toolkit
levels.blurb: Reach for utility types, assertions, and tsconfig like a confident junior dev.

questions.prompt: Which description of TypeScript is the most accurate?
choices: A CSS preprocessor that adds variables and mixins
JavaScript with added types, compiled to plain JavaScript
A database query language for Node.js servers
A new browser language that replaces JavaScript completely
questions.hint: Think about how TypeScript relates to the JavaScript you already know.
questions.explain: TypeScript is a superset of JavaScript: it adds types on top, checks them, and then outputs regular JavaScript that any browser or Node.js can run.

questions.prompt: When does TypeScript usually report a type error to you?
choices: Only when a user clicks a button
Never, it only formats your code
Only after the code crashes in production
While you write or compile the code
questions.hint: TypeScript checks your code without running it.
questions.explain: TypeScript checks types statically, so your editor and the `tsc` compiler can warn you before the program ever runs. That is how it saves you from many runtime bugs.

questions.prompt: Which kind of bug is TypeScript most likely to catch for you?
choices: A button color that looks too bright in dark mode
A server that is down for maintenance
A slow network request to an API
questions.hint: TypeScript knows the shape of your values, not the outside world.
questions.explain: Because TypeScript knows which properties an object has, it flags `user.nmae` as a property that does not exist. Network speed, servers, and design taste are outside what a type checker can see.

questions.prompt: Which of these are real benefits of using TypeScript? Select all that apply.
choices: Catching many mistakes before the code runs
Faster code execution in the browser
questions.hint: Think about what is left after the types are removed.
questions.explain: TypeScript improves the developer experience: autocomplete, early error checks, and confident refactors. It does not make the output run faster, because the types are erased.

questions.prompt: Browsers can run `.ts` files directly, so you never need to compile or strip the types first.
questions.hint: What happens to annotations before code reaches the browser?
questions.explain: Browsers only understand JavaScript. A tool such as `tsc`, Vite, or esbuild turns TypeScript into JavaScript first.

questions.prompt: In this line, what is the `: number` part called?
questions.code: let age: number = 30;
questions.hint: It is how you write down the type you intend a variable to have.
questions.explain: A type annotation is the `: Type` you write after a name. It tells TypeScript what type the variable must hold, so it can check every assignment.

questions.prompt: What happens when TypeScript checks this code?
questions.code:
let city: string = "Paris";
city = 42;
choices: An error: a `number` is not assignable to `string`
It compiles, and `city` becomes a number
It compiles, and `42` is turned into `"42"`
An error: `city` cannot be reassigned after it is set
questions.hint: Look at the type that `city` was annotated with.
questions.explain: Once `city` is annotated as `string`, every later assignment must also be a string. TypeScript reports the mismatch instead of silently converting the value. Reassigning is fine, because `city` is a `let`.

questions.prompt: Fill in the parameter type that makes this function compile (one lowercase word).
questions.hint: Which kind of value has a `toUpperCase` method?
questions.explain: `toUpperCase` is a string method, so `text` must be a `string`. With that annotation, TypeScript also checks that every caller passes text.

questions.prompt: Which file extension do regular TypeScript source files use?
questions.hint: Plain JavaScript files use `.js`. TypeScript follows the same pattern.
questions.explain: TypeScript files end in `.ts` (or `.tsx` when they contain JSX). The compiler reads them and writes `.js` files.

questions.prompt: Which type should you use for a value that is either `true` or `false`?
questions.hint: Run `typeof true` in JavaScript and see which name it prints.
questions.explain: The TypeScript primitive for `true` and `false` is `boolean`. Other languages use `bool`, but in TypeScript that name does not exist.

questions.prompt: What type does TypeScript infer for `count`?
questions.code: let count = 10;
questions.hint: TypeScript looks at the starting value. Also notice the `let`.
questions.explain: TypeScript infers the type from the initial value. Because `let` allows reassignment, it widens `10` to the general `number` type.

questions.prompt: Why does TypeScript report an error on this line?
questions.code: let isDone: boolean = "false";
questions.hint: Look closely at the quotes.
questions.explain: The quotes make `"false"` a string. A `boolean` variable needs the real values `true` or `false`, written without quotes.

questions.prompt: What type does TypeScript infer for `names`?
questions.code: const names = ["Ada", "Grace", "Linus"];
questions.hint: Every element is the same kind of value.
questions.explain: An array literal full of strings is inferred as `string[]`, an array of strings. TypeScript does not guess a tuple like `[string]` here, because arrays can grow.

questions.prompt: You do not need to annotate every variable, because TypeScript can infer many types from their initial values.
questions.hint: Remember what happened with `let count = 10;`.
questions.explain: Type inference means TypeScript figures out types for you in many places. Many developers annotate function parameters and let inference handle simple local variables.

questions.prompt: Which of these are valid ways to type an array of numbers? Select all that apply.
questions.hint: Two of these forms appear in real TypeScript code every day.
questions.explain: `number[]` and `Array<number>` mean the same thing. The other two are not TypeScript syntax for arrays.

questions.prompt: Type the name of the official TypeScript compiler command (three lowercase letters).
questions.hint: It is the command you run with `npx` after you install the `typescript` package.
questions.explain: `tsc` checks your types and compiles `.ts` files to `.js`. You can run it with `npx tsc` in a project that has TypeScript installed.

questions.prompt: What happens to your type annotations when TypeScript compiles a file to JavaScript?
choices: They are removed, leaving plain JavaScript
They are kept as comments for the browser
They are converted into JSON files
They become runtime checks that throw errors
questions.hint: Browsers do not understand type annotations.
questions.explain: Types exist only while you develop. The compiler erases them, so the output is ordinary JavaScript with no extra runtime type checks.

questions.prompt: What does TypeScript say about the last line?
questions.code:
let scores: number[] = [90, 85];
scores.push("100");
choices: An error: `push` does not exist on arrays
It compiles, and the array now holds mixed types
questions.hint: What kind of items did you promise this array would hold?
questions.explain: A `number[]` only accepts numbers, so `push` expects a `number`. Passing the string `"100"` is reported, which keeps the array consistent.

questions.prompt: Which type means exactly the same as `string[]`?
questions.hint: One form uses square brackets, the other uses angle brackets.
questions.explain: `Array<string>` is the generic way to write `string[]`; both mean an array of any length that holds strings. `[string]` is different: it is a tuple with exactly one item.

questions.prompt: What does TypeScript do with the call on the last line?
choices: Ignores the call because it has no annotation
Reports a type error for the argument
questions.hint: Check the type of the parameter `n`.
questions.explain: The parameter `n` is annotated as `number`, so every call must pass a number. TypeScript catches the string argument before it can cause odd results at runtime.

questions.prompt: In this function, which part declares the return type?
choices: The `: number` written after the parameter `a`
The `: number` after the closing parenthesis
questions.hint: The return type comes after the whole parameter list.
questions.explain: A return type annotation goes right after the parameter list, before the `{`. TypeScript then checks that every `return` gives back a value of that type.

questions.prompt: Which of these lines compile without errors? Select all that apply.
questions.hint: Check that each value matches its annotation. Quotes always make a string.
questions.explain: The quotes make `"30"` a string, so it does not fit `number`. The other lines match. `9.99` is a `number` too, because TypeScript uses one type for whole and decimal numbers.

questions.prompt: With `strict: true`, the line `let title: string = null;` compiles without errors.
questions.hint: In strict mode, `null` is its own type.
questions.explain: Strict mode turns on `strictNullChecks`, so `null` is not part of `string`. If a value can be missing, you say so explicitly with `string | null`.

questions.prompt: Type the file extension for a TypeScript file that contains JSX, such as a React component. Include the leading dot.
questions.hint: JavaScript uses `.jsx` for this. TypeScript follows the same idea.
questions.explain: Files with JSX use `.tsx`, and other TypeScript files use `.ts`. The extra `x` tells the compiler to expect JSX tags like `<Button />`.

questions.prompt: Why does TypeScript report an error on `u`?
choices: Interfaces can only be used with classes, not objects
questions.hint: Compare the object with the interface, property by property.
questions.explain: Every property in an interface is required unless you mark it optional. The object has `name` but no `age`, so it does not match `User`.

questions.prompt: An `interface` creates JavaScript code that still exists when your program runs.
questions.hint: What happens to types during compilation?
questions.explain: Interfaces are type-only. The compiler erases them completely, so they add nothing to your JavaScript bundle.

questions.prompt: What does TypeScript report here?
choices: No error, extra properties are always fine
An error: `email` does not exist in type `User`
An error: `age` must be a string
No error, and `email` is added to the `User` interface
questions.hint: The object literal has something the interface never mentioned.
questions.explain: When you assign an object literal directly to a typed variable, TypeScript checks for unknown properties. This "excess property check" catches typos and leftover fields.

questions.prompt: Which line correctly declares an optional `nickname` property inside an interface?
questions.hint: Optional function parameters use the same mark in the same place.
questions.explain: Write `?` after the property name to make it optional. Objects can then leave `nickname` out completely.

questions.prompt: With `strict: true`, what is the type of `s.theme`?
questions.hint: An optional property might not be there at all.
questions.explain: Because `theme` is optional, reading it can give you `undefined`. TypeScript adds `undefined` to the type so you remember to handle that case.

questions.prompt: Given `interface Contact { name: string; email?: string }`, which objects are valid `Contact` values? Select all that apply.
questions.hint: One property is required and must be a string; the other is optional.
questions.explain: `name` is required and must be a `string`; `email` may be left out. So `{ name: "Ada" }` and the object with both properties match. The others miss `name` or give it the wrong type.

questions.prompt: What is the type of `pair[1]`?
questions.code: let pair: [string, number] = ["age", 30];
questions.hint: In a tuple, each position has its own type. Indexes start at 0.
questions.explain: A tuple fixes the type of each position. Position `0` is a `string` and position `1` is a `number`.

questions.prompt: Fill in the keyword that gives `Admin` every property of `User` (one lowercase word).
questions.hint: Classes use the same keyword to build on a parent class.
questions.explain: `interface Admin extends User` copies all properties of `User` into `Admin` and then adds `role`. An `Admin` object needs every property from both.

questions.prompt: How do you type a variable that holds a list of `User` objects?
questions.hint: It works just like `string[]`.
questions.explain: Add `[]` after any type to get an array of it. `User[]` is an array of any length where every item is a `User`.

questions.prompt: What does the parameter type mean here?
choices: `user` must be a string, and `name` is its label
`user` can be any value at all
`user` must be an object with a string `name`
questions.hint: Curly braces in a type position describe an object shape.
questions.explain: You can write an object type inline, without an interface. `{ name: string }` means any object that has a `name` property of type `string`.

questions.prompt: Which properties does an `Admin` object need?
questions.hint: `extends` means "everything from the parent, plus more".
questions.explain: An interface that `extends` another gets all of its properties and then adds its own. So an `Admin` needs `name`, `age`, and `role`.

questions.prompt: TypeScript compares object types by their shape (their properties), not by the name of the interface they came from.
questions.hint: If it has the right properties, does the name matter?
questions.explain: TypeScript uses structural typing. Any object with the required properties fits a type, even if it was never declared with that interface name.

questions.prompt: You want to name the tuple type `[number, number]` as `Coords`. Which line does that?
questions.hint: A type alias uses a keyword and an equals sign.
questions.explain: The `type` keyword can name any type, including tuples. Interfaces do not use `=`, and `let` creates a variable, not a type.

questions.prompt: Does `let pair: [string, number] = [30, "age"];` compile?
choices: Yes, because both values are allowed in the tuple
No, tuples can only hold one type
No, the values are in the wrong order
Yes, tuples accept their values in any order
questions.hint: A tuple is like a numbered form: each slot expects something specific.
questions.explain: Order matters in a tuple. Position `0` must be a `string` and position `1` a `number`, so `[30, "age"]` does not match.

questions.prompt: Which keywords can you use to give a name to an object type like `{ id: number }`? Select all that apply.
questions.hint: Think about the two ways you have named types in this level.
questions.explain: Both `interface Item { id: number }` and `type Item = { id: number }` name an object type. TypeScript has no `struct` keyword, and `object` is a type, not a way to declare one.

questions.prompt: Type the modifier keyword that stops a property from being changed after the object is created (one lowercase word).
questions.hint: It describes something you can read but not write.
questions.explain: `readonly` marks a property as not reassignable, for example `readonly id: number`. TypeScript reports any later assignment to it.

questions.prompt: What does the line `type UserId = string;` create?
choices: A variable that holds the text `"string"`
A new name for the `string` type
A runtime check that values are strings
questions.hint: The keyword is `type`, not `let` or `class`.
questions.explain: A type alias gives a name to any type. `UserId` is still a `string`, but the name makes your code easier to read.

questions.prompt: What is the type of `order.customer.name`?
questions.hint: Follow the path through the nested object.
questions.explain: Object types can be nested. `customer` is an object type, and its `name` property is a `string`.

questions.prompt: Given `interface Box { size?: number }`, the line `const b: Box = {};` compiles without errors.
questions.hint: Is there any required property in `Box`?
questions.explain: The only property is optional, so an empty object is a valid `Box`. Optional properties may be left out entirely.

questions.prompt: What happens on the last line?
choices: An error: `x` is a read-only property
It compiles, but `y` becomes read-only too
questions.hint: Look at the word in front of `x`.
questions.explain: `readonly` means the property can be set when the object is created but not changed later. Note that `const` only stops reassigning `p` itself, not its properties.

questions.prompt: What does TypeScript say about `list.push("b")`?
questions.code:
const list: readonly string[] = ["a"];
list.push("b");
choices: It compiles, because `const` only protects the variable
It compiles and adds `"b"` to the list
An error: `push` does not exist on a read-only array
An error: `"b"` is not a string
questions.hint: What does `readonly` promise about this array?
questions.explain: A `readonly string[]` has no methods that change it, such as `push` or `splice`. This is stronger than `const`, which only stops you from reassigning `list` itself.

questions.prompt: What does this type describe?
questions.code: type Stock = { [product: string]: number };
choices: An object whose string keys all map to numbers
An object with exactly one key called `product`
A function that takes a string and returns a number
questions.hint: The square brackets describe the keys, not one specific key.
questions.explain: This is an index signature. It says the object can have any string keys, and every value must be a `number`, like `{ apples: 3, pears: 7 }`.

questions.prompt: Which statements about tuple types are true? Select all that apply.
choices: They are a separate runtime data type from arrays
Every element must have the same type
They have a fixed number of positions
Each position can have its own type
questions.hint: At runtime, a tuple is just a normal JavaScript value you already know.
questions.explain: A tuple describes an array with a known length and a known type at each position. At runtime it is still a plain JavaScript array.

questions.prompt: Fill in a tuple type with exactly two positions: a `number` first, then a `boolean`.
questions.code: let answer: ____ = [42, true];
questions.hint: Use square brackets and list one type for each position, in order.
questions.explain: A tuple type lists the type of each position inside square brackets: `[number, boolean]`. Writing `(number | boolean)[]` would allow any length and any order.

questions.prompt: In the annotation `let id: string | number;`, what does the `|` mean?
choices: `id` is a bitwise OR of two values
`id` can hold either a `string` or a `number`
`id` must be a string and a number at once
questions.hint: Read `|` out loud as "or".
questions.explain: A union type lists the types a value may have. `string | number` accepts either kind, so `id = "a1"` and `id = 7` are both fine.

questions.prompt: What does TypeScript report on the last line?
choices: No error, any string is allowed
An error: `"huge"` is not a valid `Size`
questions.hint: Check the exact list of allowed values.
questions.explain: A union of string literals allows only those exact strings. This is a great way to catch typos in things like sizes, statuses, or directions.

questions.prompt: What types does TypeScript infer for `a` and `b`?
questions.code:
let a = "hi";
const b = "hi";
questions.hint: Which one can never change its value?
questions.explain: A `const` can never be reassigned, so TypeScript keeps the exact literal type `"hi"`. A `let` might change later, so it is widened to `string`.

questions.prompt: What is the value of `Color.Green`?
questions.hint: Numeric enums start counting at zero.
questions.explain: Without explicit values, enum members are numbered from `0`. So `Red` is `0`, `Green` is `1`, and `Blue` is `2`.

questions.prompt: An `enum` member can have a string value, as in `enum Dir { Up = "UP", Down = "DOWN" }`.
questions.hint: Enums are not limited to automatic numbers.
questions.explain: This is a string enum, and it is valid TypeScript. Each member must get its string value explicitly, because strings cannot count up on their own.

questions.prompt: Why do many teams prefer `type Direction = "up" | "down"` over an `enum`?
choices: A literal union adds no code to the compiled output
Enums cannot be used in function parameters
Enums are not allowed when the `strict` option is on
Literal unions run faster than numbers
questions.hint: Think about what each one leaves behind in the compiled JavaScript.
questions.explain: A union of string literals is erased at compile time, and you can pass plain strings like `"up"`. A regular `enum` generates a JavaScript object. Both are valid; the union is simply lighter.

questions.prompt: Which values can a variable of type `"yes" | "no" | 1` hold? Select all that apply.
questions.hint: Only values listed in the union are allowed.
questions.explain: A union of literal types allows exactly the values it lists. `"yes"`, `"no"`, and `1` fit; `"maybe"` and `2` do not.

questions.prompt: Fill in the operator that checks a value's runtime type (one lowercase word).
questions.hint: It is a JavaScript operator that returns a type name as a string.
questions.explain: `typeof value` returns a string like `"string"` or `"number"`. TypeScript uses this check to narrow the type of `value`.

questions.prompt: The code `let value: string | number = 42; value = true;` compiles without errors.
questions.hint: Is `boolean` in the union?
questions.explain: The union allows only `string` or `number`. Assigning `true`, a `boolean`, is an error.

questions.prompt: Why does TypeScript report an error in this function?
choices: The function needs a return type annotation first
`v` might be a number, which has no `length`
questions.hint: You can only use what every member of the union has.
questions.explain: On a union, you may only use members that all the types share. Strings have `length` but numbers do not, so you need to narrow `v` first.

questions.prompt: Inside the `if` block, what is the type of `v`?
questions.hint: The `if` condition tells TypeScript something about `v`.
questions.explain: A `typeof` check narrows the union. Inside the block `v` is `string`, and after it TypeScript knows only `number` is left, so `toFixed` is allowed.

questions.prompt: Why is `name.toUpperCase()` allowed here under `strict: true`?
choices: Strict mode allows calling methods on `undefined`
questions.hint: What value would make `if (name)` false?
questions.explain: This is truthiness narrowing. `undefined` is falsy, so inside the `if` block TypeScript knows `name` is a `string`.

questions.prompt: This check is meant to skip only missing counts. Which real number does it also skip by accident?
questions.hint: Which number is falsy in JavaScript?
questions.explain: `0` is falsy, so `if (count)` treats it like a missing value. Use `if (count !== undefined)` when zero is a valid value.

questions.prompt: In the `else` branch, what is the type of `pet`?
questions.hint: If `pet` does not have `meow`, which type is left?
questions.explain: The `in` operator checks whether a property exists. If `"meow"` is not in `pet`, TypeScript narrows it to `Dog` in the `else` branch.

questions.prompt: Which strings can the JavaScript `typeof` operator return, so you can use them in narrowing checks? Select all that apply.
questions.hint: For an array, `typeof` gives a more general answer.
questions.explain: `typeof` returns strings like `"string"`, `"number"`, `"boolean"`, and `"object"`. Arrays give `"object"`, which is why you use `Array.isArray` for them, and whole numbers give `"number"`.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank so TypeScript knows `r` has a `message` property. Type just the word, without quotes.
questions.hint: Find the member of the union that has `message`.
questions.explain: Only the member with `status: "error"` has `message`. Checking `r.status === "error"` narrows `r` to that member, so `r.message` is allowed.

questions.prompt: Which type allows the mixed array `[1, "two", 3]`?
questions.hint: Each item, not the whole array, can be one type or the other.
questions.explain: `(string | number)[]` is an array where each item may be a string or a number. `string[] | number[]` means the whole array is all strings or all numbers.

questions.prompt: Does this function compile?
choices: No, you must narrow `v` before using any property
Yes, but only if `v` is a string at runtime
Yes, both types have a `length` property
questions.hint: Check whether each member of the union has `length`.
questions.explain: Members shared by every type in a union are safe to use without narrowing. Both strings and arrays have a `length` number.

questions.prompt: At the `// here` comment, TypeScript treats `value` as a `number`.
questions.hint: Which values leave the function early?
questions.explain: Every string returns early, so only numbers reach `// here`. TypeScript follows the `return` and narrows `value` to `number` for the rest of the function.

questions.prompt: Which of these checks does TypeScript understand for narrowing a type? Select all that apply.
choices: A comment like `// value is a string`
questions.hint: TypeScript reads code, not comments.
questions.explain: Truthiness checks, `Array.isArray`, and equality checks like `=== null` are real code that TypeScript follows to narrow types. Comments are ignored by the type checker.

questions.prompt: Inside the `if` block, what is the type of `x`?
questions.hint: `Array.isArray` tells you whether the value is an array.
questions.explain: TypeScript understands `Array.isArray`, so it narrows `x` to `string[]` inside the block. After the block, only `string` is left.

questions.prompt: With `strict: true`, why does this function report an error?
questions.hint: What would happen at runtime if someone passed `null`?
questions.explain: Calling a method on `null` crashes at runtime, so strict mode makes you handle it. Add a check like `if (s === null) return "";` and the rest of the function is safe.

questions.prompt: Inside the `if` block, which property can you safely read from `s`?
questions.hint: The `kind` value tells you exactly which object you have.
questions.explain: Each member has a literal `kind` property, so checking it narrows `s` to the circle type. This pattern is called a discriminated union.

questions.prompt: Fill in the operator that checks whether a property exists on an object (one lowercase word).
questions.hint: It is a two-letter JavaScript keyword.
questions.explain: The `in` operator returns `true` when the property exists. TypeScript narrows `shape` to the union members that have `radius`.

questions.prompt: What does the `void` return type tell you about `log`?
choices: It does not return a useful value
It returns the message it logs
questions.hint: Look at what the function body actually returns.
questions.explain: `void` means the function is used for its side effect, not for a return value. It is the usual return type for functions like loggers and event handlers.

questions.prompt: Given `function greet(name: string, title?: string)`, which call causes an error?
questions.hint: Only one of the parameters has a `?`.
questions.explain: `title` is optional, but `name` is required. Calling `greet()` with no arguments leaves out the required `name`.

questions.prompt: What type does TypeScript infer for the parameter `times`?
questions.hint: TypeScript looks at the default value.
questions.explain: A default value lets TypeScript infer the parameter type, here `number`. The parameter also becomes optional for callers.

questions.prompt: With `strict: true`, TypeScript reports an error for this function.
questions.hint: What type would `name` get without an annotation?
questions.explain: Strict mode includes `noImplicitAny`. The parameter `name` would silently become `any`, so TypeScript asks you to add an annotation like `name: string`.

questions.prompt: Which is the correct way to type a rest parameter that collects numbers?
questions.hint: The rest parameter collects many values into one array.
questions.explain: A rest parameter gathers the remaining arguments into an array, so its type is an array type like `number[]`.

questions.prompt: What does TypeScript report for the last line?
choices: An error: a `Promise<string>` is not a `string`
No error, because `async` functions return plain values
An error: `async` functions cannot have a return type
questions.hint: Look at the return type on the first line.
questions.explain: Calling an `async` function gives you a promise, here a `Promise<string>`. To get the `string` itself, write `await fetchName()` inside another `async` function.

questions.prompt: Given `type Handler = (event: string) => void;`, which functions can be assigned to a `Handler` variable? Select all that apply.
questions.hint: A function may ignore arguments it gets, but it cannot demand extra ones or the wrong type.
questions.explain: A function that takes a `string`, or takes no parameters at all, can safely be called with one string. A function that wants a `number`, or needs a second argument, would break when called as a `Handler`.

questions.prompt: Fill in the return type for a function that never returns at all, because it always throws (one lowercase word).
questions.hint: No value of this type can ever exist.
questions.explain: `never` means a function never finishes normally, for example because it always throws. `void` is for functions that do finish but return nothing useful.

questions.prompt: What does TypeScript report for the second line?
questions.code:
let data: any = "hello";
data.foo.bar();
choices: An error: `foo` does not exist on type `string`
No error, and the code is safe at runtime
An error: `any` values cannot have properties
No error, because `any` turns off type checking
questions.hint: Think of `any` as telling TypeScript "trust me".
questions.explain: With `any`, TypeScript stops checking, so this compiles. At runtime it would crash, which is why `any` should be used sparingly.

questions.prompt: What type does TypeScript infer for `n` inside the arrow function?
questions.code: const doubled = [1, 2, 3].map((n) => n * 2);
questions.hint: TypeScript knows what kind of array `map` is called on.
questions.explain: This is contextual typing. Because the array is `number[]`, TypeScript knows the callback receives a `number`, so you do not need to annotate `n`.

questions.prompt: What return type does TypeScript infer for `parse`?
questions.hint: Look at every `return` statement.
questions.explain: TypeScript combines the types of all `return` statements. One returns `null` and the other returns a `number`, so the result is `number | null`. Nothing returns `undefined` here.

questions.prompt: You receive data from `JSON.parse` and are not sure of its shape. Which type is the safest choice for it?
questions.hint: You want TypeScript to make you check the data before you use it.
questions.explain: `unknown` accepts any value but forces you to narrow it before use. `any` and `Record<string, any>` let you use the data without checks, so mistakes slip through.

questions.prompt: You have `const x: unknown`. Which of these let you safely use `x` as a string? Select all that apply.
choices: Read `x.length` first to see if it exists
questions.hint: You must narrow `unknown` before touching any property.
questions.explain: Both `typeof` checks narrow `x` to `string` for the code that follows. Using a property or method directly on `unknown` is an error.

questions.prompt: `getUser()` returns `Promise<User>`. In this code, the type of `user` is `User`.
questions.hint: What does `await` take out of a promise?
questions.explain: `await` unwraps the promise, so `user` is `User`, not `Promise<User>`. That is why `user.name` works without errors.

questions.prompt: What type does TypeScript infer for `n`?
questions.hint: TypeScript works out `T` from the argument you pass.
questions.explain: The argument is a `number[]`, so TypeScript infers `T` as `number`. The return type `T` then becomes `number`.

questions.prompt: Fill in a primitive type argument so that the last line compiles (one lowercase word).
questions.hint: What kind of value is pushed on the last line?
questions.explain: You can pass a type argument yourself with `<...>`. With `makeList<string>()`, `T` becomes `string`, so `names` is a `string[]` and pushing `"Ada"` is allowed.

questions.prompt: What does TypeScript report for the second line?
questions.code:
let input: unknown = "hello";
input.toUpperCase();
choices: An error: `toUpperCase` is not a function
No error, because `input` holds a string
questions.hint: `unknown` makes you prove what a value is before you use it.
questions.explain: You cannot use an `unknown` value directly. Narrow it first, for example with `if (typeof input === "string")`, and then string methods are allowed.

questions.prompt: What does `type MathOp = (a: number, b: number) => number;` describe?
choices: A function from two numbers to a number
An object with the properties `a` and `b`
A function that returns two numbers
questions.hint: The arrow separates the parameters from the return type.
questions.explain: A function type lists the parameters in parentheses, then `=>`, then the return type. Any function like `(x, y) => x + y` fits `MathOp`.

questions.prompt: Generics let one function work with many types while still keeping track of the specific type used.
questions.hint: Remember how `firstItem([10, 20, 30])` returned a `number`.
questions.explain: Unlike `any`, a generic remembers the type you passed in. You get reuse and type safety together.

questions.prompt: In `function wrap<T>(value: T)`, what does `<T>` declare?
choices: A type parameter, filled in at each call
A variable named `T` that holds the value passed in
An HTML tag that wraps the value
questions.hint: It works like a function parameter, but for types.
questions.explain: Generics use type parameters. Each call can fill `T` with a different type, and TypeScript keeps track of it.

questions.prompt: Why does TypeScript report an error here?
choices: Interfaces cannot have type parameters like `T`
questions.hint: Replace `T` with `string` in your head.
questions.explain: Writing `Box<string>` fills `T` with `string`, so `value` must be a string. The number `42` does not fit.

questions.prompt: Which call causes an error?
questions.hint: `extends` here means "must have at least this shape".
questions.explain: The constraint says `T` must have a `length` number. Strings and arrays do, but a plain number does not.

questions.prompt: Which statements about the `any` type are true? Select all that apply.
choices: TypeScript still checks property names on `any` values
It is safer than `unknown` for outside data
It turns off type checking for that value
An `any` value can be assigned to a variable of almost any type
questions.hint: `any` is often called an escape hatch.
questions.explain: `any` disables checks: you can read any property and assign it anywhere. That freedom is risky, so `unknown` is the safer choice for outside data.

questions.prompt: Fill in the built-in generic type name that an `async` function returns (one word, capitalized).
questions.hint: An `async` function always gives you one of these.
questions.explain: Every `async` function returns a `Promise`. `Promise<number>` means that awaiting it gives you a `number`.

questions.prompt: What does `Partial<User>` do?
choices: Keeps only the first property of `User`
questions.hint: The call passes only some of the properties.
questions.explain: `Partial<T>` creates a type where every property is optional. It is handy for update functions that receive only the fields that changed.

questions.prompt: Which type is `Preview` equal to?
questions.hint: `Pick` keeps only the keys you name.
questions.explain: `Pick<T, Keys>` builds a new type with just the listed properties. Here it keeps only `title`, with its original type.

questions.prompt: Writing `type Short = Omit<User, "age">` leaves the original `User` type unchanged.
questions.hint: Utility types build new types from old ones.
questions.explain: Utility types never modify their input. `Short` is a brand-new type, and `User` still has every property it had before.

questions.prompt: Which properties does `NewTodo` have?
choices: None, it is an empty type
questions.hint: `Omit` is the opposite of `Pick`.
questions.explain: `Omit<T, Keys>` copies a type without the listed properties. It is perfect for "create" data where the server assigns the `id`.

questions.prompt: What does the type of `scores` describe?
choices: A function from a string to a number
An array of strings and numbers
An object with string keys and number values
A tuple that holds one string and then one number
questions.hint: The first type argument is for keys, the second for values.
questions.explain: `Record<Keys, Value>` describes an object where each key maps to a value of one type. It is a tidy way to type lookup tables.

questions.prompt: Which utility type makes all optional properties of a type required?
questions.hint: Its name is the opposite of "optional".
questions.explain: `Required<T>` removes the `?` from every property. It is the opposite of `Partial<T>`.

questions.prompt: Given `interface Todo { id: number; title: string; done: boolean }`, which types include a `title` property? Select all that apply.
questions.hint: `Pick` keeps the listed keys; `Omit` removes them.
questions.explain: Picking `"title"` keeps it, and omitting only `"id"` keeps it too. Omitting `"title"` removes it, and picking only `"id"` never includes it.

questions.prompt: Type the usual file name of a TypeScript project's config file, including the extension.
questions.hint: It sits in the project root, next to `package.json`.
questions.explain: `tsconfig.json` sits at the project root. It tells `tsc` which files to check and which `compilerOptions` to use.

questions.prompt: What does a `.d.ts` file contain?
choices: Compiled JavaScript that is ready for the browser
Unit tests for your TypeScript code
Type declarations only, with no runtime code
questions.hint: Library authors ship these files so editors know an API's types.
questions.explain: Declaration files describe the types of code that lives somewhere else, usually a JavaScript library. They contain no implementation.

questions.prompt: You install a JavaScript library that ships without types. Where do community-made types usually come from?
choices: You must rewrite the library in TypeScript
TypeScript generates them by reading the library's README
questions.hint: Look for a scoped npm package.
questions.explain: The DefinitelyTyped project publishes types as `@types/<library>` packages. Install one, for example `npm i -D @types/lodash`, and TypeScript picks it up.

questions.prompt: What does the line `declare const API_URL: string;` tell TypeScript?
choices: Make `API_URL` a constant that cannot be read
Create a new variable with an empty string value
Read `API_URL` from the `.env` file automatically at build time
questions.hint: `declare` describes something without creating it.
questions.explain: `declare` tells TypeScript about a value that exists at runtime, for example a global set by a script tag. It produces no JavaScript.

questions.prompt: What does `as HTMLInputElement` do here?
questions.code:
const input = document.getElementById("email") as HTMLInputElement;
console.log(input.value);
choices: Changes only the type TypeScript sees
Throws an error if the element is not an input
Creates a new `<input>` element in the page
Converts the element into an input element at runtime
questions.hint: Remember that types are erased when the code compiles.
questions.explain: A type assertion only changes what TypeScript believes. If the element is missing or is not an input, nothing stops it at runtime, so use `as` only when you are sure.

questions.prompt: What does the `!` at the end of the first line do?
questions.code:
const title = document.querySelector("h1")!;
title.textContent = "Hello";
choices: Checks at runtime that the element exists
Negates the result, turning it into a boolean
Tells TypeScript the value is not `null`
questions.hint: Without it, the type would be `HTMLHeadingElement | null`.
questions.explain: The non-null assertion `!` removes `null` and `undefined` from the type. Like `as`, it is only a promise to TypeScript; if you are wrong, the code fails at runtime.

questions.prompt: Running `tsc --noEmit` checks your types without writing any JavaScript files.
questions.hint: In compiler terms, to emit means to write output files.
questions.explain: `--noEmit` tells `tsc` to report type errors but skip the output. Many projects use it in CI because another tool, like Vite, builds the JavaScript.

questions.prompt: Which of these are real options inside `compilerOptions` in `tsconfig.json`? Select all that apply.
questions.hint: One belongs to a dev server, not the compiler.
questions.explain: `strict` turns on stricter checks, `target` picks the JavaScript version to output, and `outDir` sets where compiled files go. `port` is a server setting, not a compiler option.

questions.prompt: Fill in the operator that creates a type from the value `defaults` (one lowercase word).
questions.hint: You already use this operator in `if` checks at runtime.
questions.explain: In a type position, `typeof defaults` gives the type of that value: `{ theme: string; size: number }`. It saves you from writing the same shape twice.
questions.code:
const defaults = { theme: "dark", size: 14 };

type Settings = ____ defaults;

questions.prompt: What does `"strict": true` in `tsconfig.json` do?
choices: Stops the compiler from writing any JavaScript files
Turns on a group of stricter type checks
questions.hint: It is a single switch that controls several other options.
questions.explain: `strict` enables a family of checks, including `strictNullChecks` and `noImplicitAny`. It is recommended for new projects. You can still write `any` explicitly.

questions.prompt: What happens on the last line?
choices: An error: `port` is a read-only property
An error: `8080` is not a valid port
questions.hint: The utility type wraps the whole interface.
questions.explain: `Readonly<T>` marks every property as `readonly`. The original `Config` stays the same, but `cfg` cannot be changed.

questions.prompt: Writing `value as number` converts a string into a number at runtime.
questions.hint: What happens to type syntax during compilation?
questions.explain: `as` only changes the type TypeScript sees and is erased at compile time. To convert at runtime, use a function such as `Number(value)`.

questions.prompt: What type does TypeScript infer for `roles`?
questions.code: const roles = ["admin", "editor"] as const;
questions.hint: `as const` keeps values as specific and unchangeable as possible.
questions.explain: `as const` makes the array a read-only tuple and keeps the exact literal value at each position. It is a tuple, not a general array, because the length is fixed too.

questions.prompt: What type is `UserKey`?
questions.hint: `keyof` looks at the property names, not their types.
questions.explain: `keyof` gives a union of an object type's property names. It is useful for functions that accept only valid keys.

questions.prompt: What is the type `U`?
questions.hint: `ReturnType` gives you what the function returns, not the function itself.
questions.explain: `typeof makeUser` gets the function type, and `ReturnType` extracts what it returns. Object properties are widened, so you get `string` and `boolean`.

questions.prompt: Which of these are built-in TypeScript utility types? Select all that apply.
questions.hint: One name sounds right but is not built in.
questions.explain: `Partial`, `Pick`, and `Record` ship with TypeScript. There is no built-in `Optional`; you would use `Partial` for that.

questions.prompt: Fill in the keyword so this import brings in only types and is removed from the compiled JavaScript (one lowercase word).
questions.hint: The keyword names the only kind of thing this import brings in.
questions.explain: `import type` brings in types only, and the compiler always erases it. It makes clear that the import has no runtime cost.
questions.code: import ____ { User } from "./types";
